content: 1. Water must be available from an improved water supply located on the premises of the healthcare facility. This ensures that the water source is reliable, safe, and accessible for all necessary purposes, including drinking, hygiene, and medical activities. 2. Sanitation facilities must include improved toilets that are functional, private, and accessible. These toilets should be sex-separated, dedicated for staff and patients, and equipped with facilities for menstrual hygiene management. Additionally, they must be accessible to individuals with limited mobility. 3. Hygiene standards require the availability of hand hygiene facilities at points of care. These facilities must provide water and soap and/or alcohol-based hand rubs. Handwashing stations should also be located within 5 meters of toilets and must be equipped with water and soap. 4. Healthcare waste management must ensure proper segregation of waste in consultation areas. Infectious and sharps waste must be safely treated or disposed of through methods such as autoclaving, incineration, or burial in a lined, protected pit. Off-site collection for medical waste disposal is also acceptable. 5. Environmental cleaning protocols must be in place and accessible. All staff responsible for cleaning must receive adequate training. Cleaning schedules should include protocols for cleaning floors, sinks, and spillages of blood or bodily fluids. These protocols should be observed and implemented consistently. 6. The Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator for basic WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) services in healthcare facilities includes monitoring the proportion of facilities with improved water supply, sanitation, hygiene, and waste management systems. These indicators are calculated based on survey responses and are critical for assessing service levels. 7. National data on WASH in healthcare facilities should be disaggregated by urban/rural residence, facility type (hospital/non-hospital), and management type (government/non-government). This ensures a comprehensive understanding of service coverage and gaps. 8. Facility assessment surveys, supported by international organizations, are the primary source of data for WASH in healthcare facilities. These surveys, such as the Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (SARA) and the Service Delivery Indicators survey (SDI), collect nationally representative data and are conducted periodically. 9. Core questions for monitoring WASH in healthcare facilities can be adapted for use in various tools, such as national Health Management Information Systems (HMIS). These questions assess water availability, sanitation facilities, hygiene practices, and waste management systems. 10. Water quality must be sufficient for all purposes, including drinking, food preparation, personal hygiene, medical activities, cleaning, and laundry. It should be available throughout the day and across seasons. Drinking water quality should meet standards for E. coli, total coliforms, residual chlorine, arsenic, and fluoride levels. 11. Sanitation facilities must meet specific criteria, including cleanliness, lighting, cultural appropriateness, and availability of cleaning materials. Toilets should be accessible to children and individuals with limited mobility and should include measures for vector control. 12. Hygiene promotion activities should include the availability of hygiene materials at hand hygiene facilities, infection prevention training, and regular cleaning of floors, surfaces, and toilets. Cleaning materials must be sufficient and tracked to avoid shortages. 13. Healthcare waste management systems must include proper segregation, storage, and disposal of general, infectious, and sharps waste. Waste collection and transportation should be frequent and use dedicated containers. Off-site waste treatment and disposal must follow safety protocols. 14. Additional monitoring topics may include energy availability for water pumps and medical equipment, food handling and preparation, and building design features such as ventilation, heating, and air conditioning. These factors contribute to the overall safety and functionality of healthcare facilities.
